contest_compliance.target: Pocket FM — The Fated Mate: A Werewolf Romantasy Contest
contest_compliance.bond_placement: The half-spoken vow lands in B1E01, satisfying the mission requirement that the discovery of the fated bond be the beginning of the story.
contest_compliance.comprehension_policy: The bond arrives early; understanding does not. June grasps roughly a fifth of what happened to her in B1E01 and is still assembling it at B1E12. Moving the event forward must never mean moving five episodes of explanation forward with it.
contest_compliance.possessive_lead_mechanism: Elias satisfies the possessive-male-lead requirement through inversion rather than temperament: he claimed her without asking and handed her the dangerous end of the bond in the same act. He is the only person in the series who can be compelled, and she is the one who can compel him. The claim protects her and paints a target on her simultaneously, which is the stated dramatic effect. No second possessive male is introduced.
contest_compliance.awakening_mechanism: June's transformation is becoming fluent in the borne record — learning to read scent, fear, illness and kinship as precisely as she reads a transcript. She never acquires combat power. She becomes bilingual in the world's two record systems, which is why she is dangerous.
contest_compliance.visible_clock: The moon calendar on the Hall wall carries a date from B1E03. June first changed at sixteen and has survived the three nights privately for fifteen years, but her first moon window after naming is a dated, bodily, economically brutal deadline for which she has no recognized safe room, housing slot, or benefit coverage.

pov_policy.distribution: Approximately 80/20 June to Elias across Book One, loosening toward 70/30 in later seasons.
rules: One POV per episode wherever practical. Where POV must change inside an episode, change it only at a clean scene boundary — never mid-scene, and never twice in one episode.

On a POV change, the opening sentence or two establishes the new viewpoint naturally, through what that character notices, wants, or is doing. Never use a spoken character-name header, a location slug, or any mechanical POV announcement.
One narrator performs the entire work. The prose must never depend on separate performers to distinguish viewpoints.
Elias POV exists to show Trust machinery June cannot see. It must never replay a scene already given from her side, and must never resolve his motive before Chapter Twenty.
No Elias POV before B1E12, so his ambiguity survives the acquisition runway even though he appears in B1E01.

narrator_policy.scope: Pocket FM single narrator, performing every character and both viewpoints.
narrator_policy.gender: Deliberately not locked. Narrator gender is a casting decision to be made later by auditioning platform voices against drafted episodes, not a canon rule. The prose must read equally well in either register.
narrator_policy.consequence_for_prose: Because the bride carries roughly eighty percent of the viewpoint, a female narrator may prove the more natural fit — but nothing in the writing may assume it. Do not write narration whose effect depends on the narrator's gender, and do not lean on a performed contrast between the two viewpoints.

mini_arcs.question: Something impossible walked into June's deposition and bound itself to her. What was it, what does it cost, and why will nobody explain?
mini_arcs.payoff: By B1E06 she has the mechanics she can verify — his half binds only him, he can be compelled by anyone with standing, she is entirely free, and there are nine clauses running on a timetable nobody will disclose. She still does not know why he did it.

mini_arcs.question: Can June satisfy the Articles without surrendering her own front door, and what happened to the women who could not?
mini_arcs.payoff: She defeats clause one on an 1871 definition — her first win by wording — and inside the Sewickley house finds the stewards' record of seven brides and four deaths, then meets the sister of the seventh.

mini_arcs.question: June has been reading one kind of record her whole life. Can she learn to read the other one in time?
mini_arcs.payoff: She realizes she has been reading scent unconsciously for years and starts doing it on purpose — and the cost lands immediately: a lost client, an endangered friend, and a moon date on the wall she has no safe room for.

mini_arcs.question: Can June protect Milo from clause two by handling it alone?
mini_arcs.payoff: No. She is beaten on a technicality and Milo is bound as surety — the clearest cost yet of her belief that she can carry this without help.

mini_arcs.question: Will June buy her way out at someone else's expense?
mini_arcs.payoff: She refuses the cutter's price on the record, a documented election both registers note — then discovers his exposure endangers her too, so protecting herself now means protecting him.

mini_arcs.question: Is there bad faith anywhere in this document that June can expose?
mini_arcs.payoff: No. The Articles are sincere and they worked, and the Hall votes to honor them — but Kenneth Boyle votes no, alone, giving her the first ally who chose her over an institution.

mini_arcs.question: What does the moon actually cost a woman nobody will house, and what does the truth cost the people around her?
mini_arcs.payoff: She survives the first moon night for which she has asked for help because she finally stops treating solitary survival as the only acceptable plan; Cyd then learns everything, stays, and loses a contract for it.

mini_arcs.question: Who has been holding the third copy, and can the vow be taken off the table?
mini_arcs.payoff: Delisle's parish has held it since 1871, and he refuses to witness ever again — which takes the vow off the table and makes forfeiture automatic instead.

mini_arcs.question: When June finally offers to answer, will she be allowed to?
mini_arcs.payoff: No — Elias refuses her, then tells her the whole truth: he acted to stop the clause and because he wanted her, both at once. She gets the answer she has chased for forty-seven episodes and it solves nothing.

mini_arcs.question: Is there a third outcome that is neither the vow nor forfeiture?
mini_arcs.payoff: Yes. She files Tess's case, which requires her to remain the bride, then defeats clauses one through three on their own terms in front of the woman who wrote them.

mini_arcs.question: What does winning cost, and who pays it?
mini_arcs.payoff: Named aloud and paid in full: Milo released, Marta out of office, Kenneth out of the Local, Elias barred from office forever. Three clauses struck. Six left.

required_promises: Establish the self before the bond, then break it in the same episode: a woman paid to listen, nine hundred dollars short of Friday's rent, who is very good at a job that requires her to be invisible — and who is bound to a stranger before the hour is out.

Deliver the bond as the inciting incident in B1E01, with real stakes attached and consequences that cannot be retreated from. Not a tender moment: a legal event she is professionally required to transcribe while it happens to her.
Introduce the male lead and the first charge in B1E01. Elias walks into her deposition, the attachment hits her before she has a name for it, and he speaks half a vow at her in front of witnesses.

Introduce the lineage world as a concrete, specific, dreadful mechanism rather than a lecture — the Articles as an exhibit, Marta's arithmetic, an accepted witness, the moon calendar with a date on it — and refuse to explain all of it at once.
Plant two visible countdowns: nine clauses running in a sequence nobody will disclose, and a dated full moon she has no safe room, housing slot, or benefit coverage for.
Establish the human conflict that is not about monsters: rent, a month-to-month lease, a car that will not pass inspection, and an agency whose contracts her trouble is actively destroying.
Keep June an agent every single episode. She may be forbidden to speak as a participant; she is never forbidden to act through the record.
acquisition_runway.comprehension_ceiling: By the end of B1E01 June understands roughly a fifth of what happened. She knows a stranger said something binding about her and that the room went quiet. She does not yet know what an attachment is, that his half binds only him, that he can be compelled, or why he did it — and the last of those is withheld until Chapter Twenty.

season_structure.midpoint: B1E30 — June reads the sealed original in the Trust's vault and understands the Articles are sincere, were drafted to stop a slaughter, and worked. Irreversible: every strategy she had assumed bad faith, and there is no one left to expose.
season_structure.dark_night: B1E46 and B1E47 — lawful forfeiture. Milo is taken as surety by scrupulously polite people, Delisle's refusal has closed the vow, and when June offers to answer, Elias refuses to let her. Nothing was done wrong, which is what makes it final.
season_structure.climax: B1E53 through B1E55 — in the record, before Delisle as witness to a filing rather than a vow, June reads the Articles back and defeats clauses one, two and three on their own terms against the woman who drafted them. She declines the larger win that would void the peace.
season_structure.season_resolution: Three clauses are lawfully defeated and permanently barred from execution; all nine remain visible and the operative count of six is publicly recorded. Milo is released. The price is paid aloud by four named people: Marta loses the business agency, Kenneth loses the Local, Elias is barred from office in perpetuity by his own testimony, and June elects to remain a party to the Articles.
season_structure.next_season_turn: The register shows a cut nobody reported. Vera Odell's price was paid by someone, and the deed was done to a person nobody has missed yet.

episodes.title: On the Record
episodes.location: the deposition suite, Grant Street
episodes.cold_open: Nine minutes into a probate deposition June is already having a bad morning — the witness is stalling, the fee is short, and rent is due Friday — when he reads an exhibit into the record and her own full name comes out of his mouth in the middle of a sentence about a contract signed in eighteen seventy-one.
episodes.pressure: She is the officer of the record at what turns out to be her own disposal, and she cannot stop working. Speaking as a participant voids the transcript and her contract; walking out costs her the fee she needs by Friday. The only copy of what is being said about her is the one she is being paid to produce.
progression: Scene one, the self before the bond: ordinary hostile probate work. June catches a misspoken date nobody else notices and fixes it without being asked. At the far end of the table sits a heavy woman in a windbreaker who is not a lawyer, has not been introduced, and has not stopped watching her.

Scene two, the exhibit: Pratt reads an old agreement into the record, clause by clause, in the flat voice of a man who loves documents. Nine clauses. A bride in each generation. Seven named since eighteen seventy-one. Then the eighth name, and it is hers. She keeps typing, because stopping would be worse — and the woman in the windbreaker does not look up, which is the frightening part.

Scene three, the intrusion: a man comes in from a corridor with no windows, at an hour that makes no sense, and something in June's chest turns toward him before she has his name. Pratt calls the priest at the end of the table an accepted witness. The man states his name for the record and opens a folder.

Scene four, the substitution and her one permitted act: he does not read the clause. He speaks a formal sentence directly to her instead — an offer of himself, by name, in front of a witness. Nobody explains it. June understands only the grammar, which is that it is a complete statement waiting for an answer, and she does the single thing her job allows her to do: she asks for a clarification for the record. That question is what forces the priest to say aloud, on the transcript, exactly what has just happened.
episodes.payoff: Whatever was about to happen to June stops happening: the clause is not read, interrupted lawfully by a stranger substituting a half-vow for the reading. And it is June's own professional instinct that produces the episode's decisive turn — her clarification for the record is what compels the witness to state the consequence aloud, which is the only reason she learns anything at all. She leaves with the exhibit number and one certainty: everyone in that room understood what he did except her.
episodes.end_hook: Delisle answers her question for the minutes: 'Let the record reflect. That binds only you, Mr. Marrow. Not her.' And the man who has not stopped looking at June says, 'I know.' She has to type it. Both lines. Exactly as spoken.
episodes.reveal_channel: A document read aloud into a deposition record, then a spoken legal substitution inside that same record, with the consequence announced aloud by the witness for the minutes. The entire episode is speech acts captured by a machine the protagonist is operating — the reveal cannot exist except as sound, and the closing beat is the protagonist being obliged to transcribe the thing that was just done to her.
continuity_updates: An agreement executed in 1871 between a lineage local and a family trust contains nine numbered clauses.
It requires a bride in each generation. Seven have been named since 1871; June Havlik is the eighth.
A clause takes legal effect when read into a record before an accepted witness.
Father Bram Delisle is an accepted witness.
Elias Marrow interrupted the reading of clause one by speaking the first half of a binding vow to June before that witness.
Speaking one half of the vow binds only the speaker and leaves the other party free — stated aloud on the transcript.
June's clarification for the record is what forced the consequence to be stated.
June is a subcontract deposition transcriptionist, nine hundred dollars short of Friday's rent.

contest_checklist.self_before_bond: Scene one — her ear, her precision, the fee, the invisibility the job requires. Established before anything supernatural is legible.
contest_checklist.concrete_pack_world: Delivered as threat, not lecture: an agreement that disposes of women read aloud as an exhibit, an accepted witness seated at the table, and an unintroduced woman who watches and does not intervene. No institution is explained.
contest_checklist.bond_as_inciting_incident: Scene four. The vow is the event of the episode, with legal stakes and public consequence.
contest_checklist.male_lead_and_first_charge: He enters in scene three and the attachment reaches her before his name does. He then binds himself to her in front of witnesses without asking — the claim that protects her and targets her in one gesture.
contest_checklist.visible_countdown: Nine clauses, stated aloud and countable, running in an undisclosed sequence.
contest_checklist.irreversible_hook: A man has permanently altered his own legal standing in front of her; she is the officer making the record of it; and her own question is what put it on the transcript.
contest_checklist.agent_not_victim: Her one legally permitted speech act drives the episode's turn and produces its button.

episodes.comprehension_note: June ends the episode knowing that something impossible happened in a room she was working, that a stranger did something consequential to himself on her behalf, and that nobody will explain it. She does not know what an attachment is, what a trustee is, that his half binds only him in any sense she can use, that he can be compelled, or why he did it. The listener hears the rules; June does not yet hold them.

episodes.title: Read It Back
episodes.location: the deposition suite, the stairwell, and a bus stop on Liberty Avenue
episodes.cold_open: Marta gets to him in the stairwell before June does, and what she says is not thank you — it is that he has just made every wolf in the county less safe, and from the way he takes it, she is right.
episodes.pressure: June is still the officer of the record. The transcript has to be certified and delivered within the hour, and certifying it means putting her signature under a sentence that bound a stranger to her.
progression: Scene one, the overheard argument: two authorities of incompatible codes going at each other in a concrete stairwell, and June extracting more from four minutes of it than either would have told her — his protections are gone, and an exposed trustee can be compelled, sued, and claimed by anyone with standing.

Scene two, her turn: she asks him plainly why. He answers the question asked and not the one meant — 'Because clause one should not have been read this morning.' True, complete, useless. She tells him she did not ask to be saved. He agrees with her, which is worse. This is the first thing that passes between them that is a relationship rather than an event.

Scene three, the certification: Pratt walks her through what she is signing with genuine professional pleasure, and June puts her name under the record of it because refusing would void the transcript, cost the agency the job, and change nothing.
Scene four, the bus stop: Cyd calls about tomorrow's assignment, and June lies to her for the first time, easily, in under six words.
episodes.payoff: June learns the mechanics and the price of what was done for her: his protections are stripped until the vow is answered or formally abandoned, he can be compelled by anyone with standing, and she is entirely free — which means the danger has been moved onto him and she cannot hand it back. She also certifies the record herself, which makes her a participant in her own binding.
episodes.end_hook: A voicemail from a number she does not know, played aloud at the bus stop. A woman's voice, cheerful and businesslike: 'Miss Havlik. My name is Vera Odell, I cut attachments for a living, and I already know what you'll be wanting. My price is never money. Call me when you've stopped being proud.'
episodes.reveal_channel: An overheard argument between two authorities in a stairwell, then a direct two-hander, then a voicemail played on a phone at a bus stop. Three distinct sound-native channels, none of them a silent visual.
continuity_updates: An exposed trustee can be compelled, sued, and claimed by any party with standing, until the vow is answered or formally abandoned.
Formal abandonment of a half-spoken vow is possible before completion and carries a stated price.
Elias will not state his reason for speaking, and answers only the literal question asked.
June certified the transcript of her own naming and the vow that followed it.
Vera Odell is a cutter who severs attachments; her price is always a deed, never money.
Attachments can be severed permanently, and there is a trade in doing so.
June lies to Cyd for the first time.

contest_checklist.opens_on_danger: An argument about how much less safe he has made everyone, overheard.
contest_checklist.agent_not_victim: She interrogates him directly, extracts the mechanics, and signs the certification as a considered choice rather than a defeat.
contest_checklist.romance_and_stakes_together: Their first real exchange arrives inside the discovery that his exposure is a standing liability.
contest_checklist.irreversible_ending: A cutter has priced her before she knew severance existed, and the offer is now on the record of her phone.

episodes.title: No Standing
episodes.location: the Hall on Cotter Street
episodes.cold_open: She comes to the Hall to resign from something and is told, kindly, over a plate of nut roll, that you cannot resign from a body you were never admitted to — by a woman who can smell exactly whose daughter she is while saying it.
episodes.pressure: Renunciation under lineage law was the entire plan, and it is nine in the morning and the plan is already gone. Behind her on the wall is a paper calendar with a date circled in red that everyone in the building has organized their month around.
progression: Scene one, the ask: June asks for the renunciation form. Yolanda goes to get it, comes back without it, and has to say out loud that there is no entry to renounce. Around them the Hall does its ordinary business — dues, the housing roster, who needs a safe room this cycle, whose employer has stopped believing them about the three nights.

Scene two, the ledger: they go through the bound roster by hand, aloud, because the Hall has never trusted the app. Her mother's line has been closed with a date and a notation. June was never opened at all. Milo, hovering, cannot reconcile his own nose against his own screen.

Scene three, the calendar: June says she already knows what the red circle means to her body. Kenneth shows her what membership would have meant around it — a safe room, an outside lock, an attendant, a housing slot, and wage coverage — and that none of those collective protections exists for someone omitted from the roster.
episodes.payoff: June learns the specific mechanism of her helplessness and that it is a paper mechanism only. She is a wolf by blood with no membership, no vote, no benefits, and no standing to renounce anything — while every member in the building carries an unalterable record of her kinship in their own bodies. And she learns the date.
episodes.end_hook: Yolanda closes the ledger, checks that the door is shut, and says quietly that there is something June should understand about the roster: it has a gap in it, and she has been the one keeping the gap for nineteen years.
episodes.reveal_channel: A bound paper ledger read aloud page by page, with the crucial fact arriving as an absence somebody has to say out loud; a wall calendar described by the person who has to explain what the circle means; and a confession lowered to a near-whisper after a door is checked.
continuity_updates: June was never initiated and has no membership, vote, benefits, or standing to renounce.
Her mother's roster line was closed with a date and a notation when she left the Hall.
Members identify blood kin by scent; kinship is a fact no filing can alter.
Members change on the three nights bracketing the full moon, involuntarily, on a public calendar.
The Local maintains safe rooms, a housing roster, dues, benefits and a burial fund because members are predictably incapacitated three nights a month.
June has changed privately for years but has no recognized safe room, housing slot, attendant, or benefit coverage. The next full moon is nineteen days away.
Local Nine's roster contains a gap Yolanda Bright has maintained for nineteen years.

contest_checklist.pack_legible_and_fearsome: The hierarchy arrives as dues, rosters, safe rooms and a circled date — precise enough to dread, and nowhere near fully explained.
contest_checklist.visible_countdown: Nineteen days to a bodily event she is uninsured, unhoused and untaught for.
contest_checklist.opens_on_danger: Her only legal exit is closed in the first forty words.
contest_checklist.irreversible_ending: A nineteen-year institutional lie is confessed to her, and she cannot un-know it.

episodes.title: The Gap
episodes.location: the Hall on Cotter Street, the business agent's office
episodes.cold_open: Yolanda gets four sentences into nineteen years before Marta opens the office door and asks, without heat, whether they would both like to come in and do this properly.
episodes.pressure: The one person about to tell June something true has been interrupted by the only person with the authority to stop her, and June can feel the fact being taken away from her in real time.
progression: Scene one, the interruption: Marta takes the conversation over courteously and completely, and Yolanda's nerve fails. The gap goes unexplained. June registers, precisely, that a fact was removed while she watched.

Scene two, the office: Marta gives her what she is willing to give — that her mother left, that the Hall let her, that Marta signed the notation herself. She does not lie, because in a closed room with a relative she cannot, and she does not insult June by trying. She refuses to say why, and does not pretend to have forgotten.

Scene three, on the record: June stops asking and starts filing. She serves a written demand for the certified copy under the exhibit number, hands it to Marta in front of Yolanda as a witness, and states the request aloud so it is heard as well as written — using both record systems at once, for the first time, without yet knowing that is what she is doing.
episodes.payoff: June learns that Marta personally signed the notation that closed her mother's line and therefore personally caused June's lack of standing — and that the refusal to explain is deliberate and permanent. She also takes her first real action of the series: a served demand that Local Nine cannot ignore, delivered in a form both lineages have to honor.
episodes.end_hook: Marta calls down the corridor after her, not unkindly: 'June. The only paper in this county with your name on it is theirs. If you want standing, you'll have to go and take it out of them.'
episodes.reveal_channel: A confession audibly cut off mid-sentence by a door opening — the interruption itself carries the reveal that someone is suppressing it — then plain dialogue across a desk, a demand read aloud as it is served, and a closing line shouted down a stairwell.
continuity_updates: Marta Havlik personally signed the notation closing June's mother's roster line, and refuses to say why her sister left.
Members cannot sustain a face-to-face lie, so Marta refuses to answer rather than attempting one.
June served a written demand for the certified copy of the Articles, witnessed and spoken aloud.
The Articles are the only instrument that legally recognizes June, making them her only available ground.
Marta actively directs June toward the Trust to seek standing.

contest_checklist.agent_not_victim: She serves a demand in both record systems simultaneously — her first act that changes the board.
contest_checklist.opens_on_danger: A truth being actively suppressed as she listens.
contest_checklist.irreversible_ending: Her own aunt tells her the only route left runs through the people who named her.

episodes.title: Twenty-Six Days
episodes.location: the Smithfield Street span, after dark
episodes.cold_open: She picks a bridge because it is the one place both lineages accept — in person, so a member can be believed, and before witnesses, so a trustee can be bound — and she is halfway across before she understands that the pull she has been calling exhaustion for four days gets stronger the closer she walks.
episodes.pressure: Twenty-six days until clause one resumes, nineteen until the moon, no standing anywhere, and her own body is doing something she did not authorize and cannot stop.
progression: Scene one, the walk out: the attachment established physically and unmistakably — not romantic yet, closer to alarming. She names it aloud as a symptom. He confirms it is real, mutual, and observable by third parties, and states flatly that it entitles neither of them to anything.

Scene two, the negotiation: she asks him to formally abandon the vow. He tells her the price of abandonment out loud before she can accept it, and it is a price she will not let him pay. She has been outmaneuvered by honesty, and it is the first time she likes him.

Scene three, the compulsion: cornered, she uses what she overheard in the stairwell. She invokes her standing over an exposed trustee and orders him to tell her why he spoke. It works. She watches a man be unable to refuse her, and it is the worst thing that has happened to her all week.
episodes.payoff: The compulsion works, and she learns two things at once: she holds coercive power over him and loathes it, and the truth is useless — he answers honestly and completely, 'Because I read clause one that morning,' which explains the act and not the man. The bond stops being a legal abstraction and becomes something she has felt and something she has abused.
episodes.end_hook: She lets go, sick with it, and tells him never to let her do that again. He straightens his cuff and says, 'Then don't ask me a question you'd rather have the answer to. There's a second half to that sentence, Miss Havlik. If you ever say it, I will have to tell you the rest.'
episodes.reveal_channel: The bond delivered as a physical gradient the character narrates while walking, so the listener feels it through distance and breath; the compulsion audible as a man's voice failing to stop itself; and the useless truth arriving as one flat sentence.
continuity_updates: The attachment is physically real, mutual, and observable by third parties; proximity intensifies it.
It confers no combat power, no telepathy, and no ability to read intent, and entitles neither party to anything.
Formal abandonment carries a stated price, disclosed before it can be accepted.
June can compel Elias while he is exposed, and has done so once.
Elias's stated reason for speaking is that he had read clause one that morning. True and incomplete.
Bridges are neutral ground because no bank owns a bridge.
Answering the vow would oblige Elias to tell her the rest.

contest_checklist.who_they_become_under_pressure: She wields power for the first time — and it is coercive power over the male lead, which is the series' inversion of the possessive-Alpha dynamic.
contest_checklist.genuine_dynamic_beyond_the_bond: Their third exchange. A negotiation, a refusal, and a warning given for her benefit against his own interest.
contest_checklist.revelation_redefining_connection: There is a second half, he knows what it costs, and he is telling her the price of asking.
contest_checklist.irreversible_ending: She now knows she can command him, and cannot un-know it.

episodes.title: Fourth Avenue
episodes.location: the Marrow Trust offices, Fourth Avenue
episodes.cold_open: She books the appointment for two in the afternoon on purpose, because at two in the afternoon the only people in a trust office are the ones who can be sued.
episodes.pressure: Clause one is suspended, not satisfied, and she does not know how long a suspension lasts. She is spending a working afternoon she cannot afford on a building where the blinds are drawn in every room.
progression: Scene one, the lobby: sunlight through plate glass, an empty reception desk, and Pratt, delighted to have a visitor who wants to talk about drafting. June exploits his one vanity, which is craft, and learns the second lineage's epistemology by watching him refuse to accept anything she says until she writes it down.

Scene two, the list: he walks her through the nine clauses in sequence — what each requires in outline, never when it falls due. She gets the shape of the whole document, and the fact that four of the seven earlier brides died under specific numbered clauses.

Scene three, the ask that fails: she asks who else holds a copy. Pratt says the Trust holds the sealed original and the Local a certified copy. Then he checks a card index, stops, and says a third holder is listed and he has never in twenty-two years been told who.
episodes.payoff: June obtains the sequence of all nine clauses in outline, learns four of seven earlier brides died under numbered clauses, confirms an unidentified third holder exists, and grasps the asymmetry she can exploit: trustees are bound by writing and cannot smell a lie, which makes them beatable on paper by a woman who makes paper for a living.

June's completion route is removed along with the coercive route.

Delisle confirms his refusal is personal and cannot be delegated as an office.
Tess reveals that forfeiture creates the standing condition her case has always needed.

Without him the vow cannot be completed.
Tess's litigation strategy anticipated forfeiture.

Constance enters June's apartment through a valid invitation from a resident.

June freely attempts to answer the vow, and Elias prevents completion without a witness.

June's first free choice to answer is made but cannot take effect.

Elias acknowledges he wrongfully overrode her physical autonomy.
A bride-filed action is the only remaining route to Milo.

Tess's bride-standing theory becomes the only operational path.

episodes.title: The Reason
episodes.location: the Sewickley house, a counted night

He cannot separate rescue from desire and asks June whether that uncertainty changes what she will do next.

He had also wanted June for two years after observing her deposition work.
He cannot truthfully rank the two motives.

episodes.title: Two Years

His attraction predates the attachment's public recognition.
He has prepared testimony that will permanently end his eligibility for office if used.

She commits to examining Tess's full case.

episodes.title: The Address
episodes.location: Polish Hill, and a post office
episodes.premise: June finally uses the forwarding address from the Sewickley house book and writes to the bride who got out ninety years ago.
episodes.payoff: She acts on the strategy she was given in episode ten, closing the runway's oldest open loop and reaching past Book One's cast for the first time.
episodes.end_hook: A reply comes back in four days, in handwriting, and the first line is: 'Do not answer him until you know what your mother took.'
episodes.primary_question: Will the released bride answer June's letter?
episodes.cold_open: June has one envelope and ninety years of silence, and the post-office clerk is about to close the window.
episodes.pressure: Contact may expose a survivor who made herself indispensable to remain free, but failing to write abandons the oldest usable precedent.
progression: June writes only what the house ledger already permits her to know and asks for no protected history.
She sends the letter and spends four days rebuilding ordinary routines rather than waiting passively.
A handwritten reply arrives warning her not to answer Elias until she knows what her mother took.
episodes.reveal_channel: June reads her outgoing letter to Cyd before mailing it, then reads the handwritten first line aloud when the reply arrives.
continuity_updates: June contacts the released bride using Nadia's forwarding address.
The released bride is alive and replies within four days.
She links completion of the vow to the protected question of what June's mother took.

episodes.title: The Unreported Cut
episodes.location: the Smithfield Street span, at dusk
episodes.premise: SEASON FINALE. June and Elias on a bridge, unmarried, the vow still half-spoken, on the same side of it for the first time.
episodes.payoff: Full closure on the season's emotional question: she neither answers the vow nor asks or compels Elias to abandon his half, and states plainly why preserving the half-bound state is an active choice rather than indecision. Nothing new is opened.
episodes.end_hook: The small forward sting: she reads Yolanda's unaccounted entry aloud to him. Somebody paid Vera Odell's price this month, and the cut was performed on a person neither register can name.
episodes.primary_question: What has June chosen for the half-spoken vow now that the immediate clauses are defeated?
episodes.cold_open: On the span, Elias asks whether June brought him there to answer, and she says no before he can finish the question.
episodes.pressure: The book must settle her election without completing an irrevocable bond, requiring Elias's excommunication, or disguising delay as indecision.
progression: June states that she will not answer the vow and will not seek or compel Elias's formal abandonment; he retains that costly choice for himself.
Elias accepts the boundary without bargaining, and they define the working alliance that follows the Book One victory.
Only after the emotional and legal resolution lands, June reads Yolanda's unaccounted severance entry aloud as a small forward sting.
episodes.reveal_channel: June's election is spoken plainly over river sound; the final sting is a registry entry read aloud, never a silent visual.
continuity_updates: The vow remains half-spoken by June's explicit election.
June and Elias end Book One allied but not bonded.
Both registers contain an unreported cut involving a person neither can name.

arc_plan.central_dramatic_question: Can June survive and defeat the first tranche of the Articles without surrendering her consent, and choose what the half-spoken vow will mean on her own terms?
arc_plan.primary_external_conflict: Clauses one through three force residence, surety, and a witnessed-vow deadline while Local Nine protects its charter and the Marrow Trust seeks institutional survival.
arc_plan.primary_emotional_arc: June moves from treating every relationship as a contract to escape toward recognizing that a debt freely chosen and reciprocally carried is not a trap.
arc_plan.primary_relationship_arc: June and Elias move from public unilateral claim and coercive asymmetry to a bounded alliance in which his motive is spoken, his desire becomes accountable action, and her refusal remains absolute.

major_character_arcs.June: Becomes fluent in both record systems, asks for help, files as the living bride, and chooses continued standing without completing the vow or seeking Elias's abandonment.
major_character_arcs.Elias: Moves from correct instrument to accountable witness, reveals both motives, and permanently gives up eligibility for office to support June's narrower victory.
major_character_arcs.Marta: Defends three hundred eleven memberships in good faith, preserves the charter, and pays by losing the business agency.
major_character_arcs.Cyd: Rejects protective secrecy, chooses informed loyalty, and absorbs a countable business loss without becoming a supernatural initiate.
major_character_arcs.Tess: Sees her bad-faith theory fail, adapts her eleven-year case, and gets it filed by the first living bride with standing.
major_character_arcs.Milo: Owns his voluntary surety choice, bears its consequence, and is released without being reduced to passive collateral.
